description: A comprehensive study of fluid behavior at rest and in motion, covering fundamental fluid properties, fluid kinematics, dynamics, pipe flow analysis, and boundary layer theory.

sections.title: Fluid Properties and Hydrostatics
sections.description: Understanding the fundamental characteristics of fluids and the physical laws governing fluids at rest.

key_concepts.explanation: States that the shear stress (tau) on a fluid element layer is directly proportional to the rate of shear strain or velocity gradient (du/dy). Fluids obeying this law are Newtonian fluids.

The phenomenon of the rise or fall of a liquid surface in a small tube relative to the adjacent general level of liquid, caused by the relative magnitudes of cohesion (intermolecular attraction) and adhesion (attraction to the solid surface).
The rate of increase of pressure in a vertically downward direction must be equal to the specific weight of the fluid at that point. It forms the basis for manometry and pressure measurement.

results: The total hydrostatic force acts through a point called the Center of Pressure.
For any submerged plane surface, the Center of Pressure is always located below or at the Center of Gravity (Centroid), never above it.

sections.title: Fluid Kinematics
sections.description: The study of fluid motion without considering the external forces that cause the motion, focusing on velocity and acceleration.

equations: Incompressible 1D Flow: A1 * V1 = A2 * V2 (Discharge Q is constant)

key_concepts.explanation: A mathematical function defined for two-dimensional, incompressible flow. The difference in the stream function between any two points gives the volumetric flow rate across a line connecting them. If it exists, it satisfies the continuity equation implicitly.
A scalar function whose negative derivative with respect to any direction gives the fluid velocity in that direction. Its existence guarantees that the flow is irrotational.

sections.title: Fluid Dynamics
sections.description: The study of fluid motion while considering the external forces (such as pressure and gravity) causing the flow.

equations: Where (P / (rho * g)) is Pressure Head, (V^2 / (2 * g)) is Kinetic/Velocity Head, and Z is Datum/Potential Head.

results: Fluid must be ideal (incompressible and non-viscous/frictionless).
Flow must be irrotational, or the equation must be applied strictly along a single streamline.
Venturimeter: Used to measure discharge. High accuracy, low head loss. Coefficient of discharge (Cd) is typically 0.95 to 0.98.
Orifice Meter: Used to measure discharge. Cheaper and takes less space, but has high head loss. Cd is typically 0.60 to 0.65.
Pitot Tube: Used to measure the local velocity of flow at a specific point by determining the stagnation pressure.

sections.title: Flow Through Pipes
sections.description: Analysis of viscous fluid flow enclosed in pipes, focusing on frictional losses and energy gradient lines.

equations: Head Loss due to friction (hf) = (f * L * V^2) / (2 * g * D)
Where 'f' is the Darcy friction factor. Note: Sometimes expressed using Fanning friction factor (f') where f = 4f'.

results: Maximum velocity is exactly twice the average velocity (Vmax = 2 * Vavg).
Darcy Friction Factor (f) depends only on Reynolds number: f = 64 / Re.
Velocity profile is flatter (logarithmic or power-law profile).
Friction factor depends on both Reynolds number and relative surface roughness.

sections.title: Boundary Layer Theory and Dimensional Analysis
sections.description: Study of the thin layer near a solid boundary where viscous effects are dominant, and the use of dimensionless numbers to scale fluid phenomena.

key_concepts.explanation: Occurs when the fluid layer closest to the solid surface is brought to rest by friction and an adverse pressure gradient (dP/dx > 0). The flow detaches from the surface, creating a wake of high turbulence and significant pressure drag.
The ratio of inertia forces to viscous forces. It is the primary parameter distinguishing between laminar and turbulent flows.
The ratio of flow velocity (V) to the local speed of sound (C). Important for compressible flows (aerodynamics). Flow is supersonic if M > 1.
